questions.stem: A theoretical (or expected) probability distribution is one whose probabilities are:

options.text: Obtained by counting the outcomes of a completed experiment
options.explanation: That describes an observed or empirical distribution, built from data already collected. A theoretical distribution is written down before data are collected.

options.text: Derived from a mathematical law based on stated assumptions, before any data are collected
options.explanation: Correct. A theoretical distribution comes from a law, such as the binomial or Poisson formula, fixed by a few assumptions and parameters, so it gives the probability of every value in advance.

options.text: Always equal for every value the variable can take
options.explanation: That is the special case of a uniform distribution, not a definition of a theoretical distribution in general.
The binomial and Poisson are theoretical distributions of discrete variables, so this is false.

readLink.label: Read: What a theoretical distribution is, §1 →

questions.stem: Which statement correctly classifies the three standard distributions of this chapter?

options.text: Binomial and Poisson are continuous; normal is discrete
options.explanation: The reverse is true. Counts of successes or events are discrete; a measurement spread over a range is continuous.

options.text: Binomial and Poisson are discrete; normal is continuous
options.explanation: Correct. The binomial counts successes and the Poisson counts occurrences, both whole numbers, so both are discrete. The normal models a continuous measurement.
The normal curve spreads probability over an interval, so it is continuous, not discrete.
The binomial and Poisson attach probability to separate whole-number values, so they are discrete.

readLink.label: Read: What a theoretical distribution is, §1 →

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of the binomial distribution?

options.text: The number of trials is fixed in advance
options.explanation: This is a genuine assumption. The binomial needs a known, fixed n.

options.text: Each trial has exactly two outcomes, success or failure
options.explanation: This is a genuine assumption. Each trial must be a Bernoulli trial.

options.text: The probability of success may change from trial to trial
options.explanation: Correct choice. This is NOT an assumption — it contradicts one. The binomial requires the success probability p to stay constant across trials, which is why sampling without replacement is not binomial.
This is a genuine assumption. One trial's result must not affect another's.

options.explanation: This is the mean, n p. A binomial variance is always below its mean, so it cannot be 6.
Correct. Variance = n p q = 20 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 4.2, which is below the mean of 6, as it must be.

options.explanation: This is the variance, n p q = 100 × 0.5 × 0.5. The standard deviation is its square root.
This is the mean, n p. The standard deviation is √(n p q).

questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed 4 times. The probability of getting at least one head is:

options.explanation: This is P(no head) = (1/2)^4 = 1/16. The question asks for at least one head, which is the complement.
This is the probability of a head on a single toss, not at least one in four.
This is one toss's chance of a head. Over four tosses at least one head is far more likely.

questions.stem: The probability that a component passes a test is 0.8, so the probability it fails is 0.2. In 5 independent tests, the probability that none fails is:

options.explanation: Correct. 'None fails' means all 5 pass: P = (0.8)^5 = 0.32768 ≈ 0.3277. Equivalently P(X = 0 failures) = q^n with q = 0.8.
This is 1 − 0.3277, the probability that at least one fails, not that none fails.
This is the single-test failure probability, not the chance of no failure in five tests.
No failures is quite possible; its probability is 0.3277, not zero.

questions.stem: A binomial distribution has mean 4 and variance 2.4. The number of trials n is:

options.explanation: This does not satisfy mean = n p. With q = variance ÷ mean = 0.6 and p = 0.4, n must be 4 ÷ 0.4 = 10.
Correct. q = variance ÷ mean = 2.4 ÷ 4 = 0.6, so p = 0.4 and n = mean ÷ p = 4 ÷ 0.4 = 10.
This is the mean itself, mistaken for n. The mean equals n p, not n.
This is p, the success probability, not the number of trials.

This rounds 4.4 up. The mode is the integer part of (n + 1)p, which is the value below it, 4.
This is (n + 1)p itself. The mode must be a whole number of successes, its integer part.

questions.stem: The Poisson distribution arises from the binomial as a limiting case when:

options.text: n is small and p is large
options.explanation: This is the opposite of the Poisson conditions. The Poisson describes rare events in many trials.

options.text: n is large, p is small and the product n p stays finite
options.explanation: Correct. As n tends to infinity and p to zero with n p = m fixed, the binomial tends to the Poisson with mean m.

options.text: n and p are both large
options.explanation: A large p with large n gives a roughly normal shape, not a Poisson.
p = 0.5 gives a symmetric binomial, which does not tend to the Poisson.

questions.stem: The number of misprints on a page is Poisson with mean 2. Taking e^(-2) = 0.1353, the probability of exactly 3 misprints on a page is:

options.explanation: This is P(X = 2) = e^(-2) × 2^2 ÷ 2! = 2 × 0.1353. The question asks for exactly 3.
This is P(X = 0) = e^(-2), the no-misprint probability.

questions.stem: In a Poisson distribution, the mean is always:

options.explanation: Not so. For a Poisson the mean and variance are the same number.
Not so. There is no gap between them in a Poisson.
Correct. A defining property of the Poisson is that its mean and variance are both equal to m.

options.text: Equal to the square root of the variance
options.explanation: The standard deviation, not the mean, is the square root of the variance. For a Poisson the mean equals the variance m, while the SD is √m.

questions.stem: Two independent Poisson variables have means 1.5 and 2.5. Taking e^(-4) = 0.0183, the probability that their sum is zero is:

options.explanation: Correct. By the additive property the sum is Poisson with mean 1.5 + 2.5 = 4, so P(sum = 0) = e^(-4) = 0.0183.
This multiplies the two separate P(0) values, e^(-1.5) × e^(-2.5), but computes them wrongly; the clean route is e^(-4).
This is e^(-2), using a mean of 2 rather than the combined mean of 4.

questions.stem: For a Poisson distribution, P(X = 1) equals P(X = 2). The mean m is:

options.explanation: With m = 1, P(1) = 0.3679 while P(2) = 0.1839; they are not equal.
Correct. The recurrence gives P(2) ÷ P(1) = m ÷ 2. Setting this ratio to 1 gives m = 2, so P(1) and P(2) are equal.
With m = 4 the ratio P(2) ÷ P(1) is 2, so P(2) is twice P(1), not equal.
With m = 0.5 the ratio is 0.25, so P(2) is a quarter of P(1).

questions.stem: Which statement about the normal distribution is correct?

options.explanation: The normal curve is perfectly symmetric, so its skewness is zero, not positive.

options.text: Its mean, median and mode are all equal
options.explanation: Correct. Because the curve is symmetric about the centre, the mean, median and mode coincide at μ.

options.text: The area under the curve is 0.5
options.explanation: The total area under any probability curve is 1; 0.5 is the area on each side of the mean.
The normal is continuous, spreading probability over an interval, not over separate points.

options.explanation: The two inflexion points sit symmetrically on either side of the mean, not at the mean itself.
Correct. The curve changes its bending exactly one standard deviation on each side of the mean.
Two standard deviations mark the 95.45% band, not the inflexion points.
Three standard deviations mark the 99.73% band, not the inflexion points.

questions.stem: For a normal distribution the area from the mean to one standard deviation (z = 0 to 1) is 0.3413. The percentage of values lying within one standard deviation of the mean is:

options.explanation: This is the area on one side only. 'Within one standard deviation' spans both sides of the mean.
Correct. The band μ − σ to μ + σ covers 2 × 0.3413 = 0.6826, that is 68.26%.
This is the two-standard-deviation band, 2 × 0.4772, not the one-σ band.
50% is the area on one entire side of the mean, not the one-σ band.

questions.stem: For a normal distribution the area from the mean to two standard deviations (z = 0 to 2) is 0.4772. The percentage of values lying within two standard deviations of the mean is:

options.explanation: This is the area on one side only. The band covers both sides of the mean.
This is the one-standard-deviation band, 2 × 0.3413, not the two-σ band.
Correct. The band μ − 2σ to μ + 2σ covers 2 × 0.4772 = 0.9544, that is 95.44%.
This is the three-standard-deviation band, not the two-σ band.

questions.stem: The area under the standard normal curve from 0 to 1 is 0.3413. The probability P(Z greater than 1) is:

options.explanation: This is the area from 0 to 1, not the tail beyond 1. Subtract it from 0.5.
Correct. P(Z greater than 1) = 0.5 − 0.3413 = 0.1587, the area in the upper tail.
This is P(Z less than 1) = 0.5 + 0.3413, the area to the left of 1, not the right.
This subtracts 0.3413 from 1 instead of from 0.5, forgetting that only half the curve lies to the right of the mean.

options.explanation: This is the area from 0 to 2 only. It omits the whole left half of the curve.
